$comment: Registry of Canadian federal and Quebec government spending sources. `access` is the field that matters for build planning: 'ckan' and 'bulk' sources need no scraping, 'pdf' sources need table extraction, 'crawl' sources need an index walk before extraction. Every entry is unverified until scripts probe it from a network that can reach these hosts.

sources.name: SEAO — Système électronique d'appel d'offres
sources.covers: Every public contract awarded in Quebec since 2009: ministries, the education network, health and social services, and municipalities. Searchable by supplier.
sources.format_notes: Yearly XML archives 'Année 2009'-'Année 2020', then monthly XML archives named in French ('Mai 2024'), running to May 2024. OCDS JSON as mensuel_/hebdo_ files from June 2021. Each XML archive is a zip of six files: Avis (notices and all bidders), Contrats (final amounts), Depenses (spending beyond contract), plus a Revisions file for each. The dataset also carries the XML and JSON format specifications as PDFs.
sources.notes: Verified against the live dataset: 418 resources, 12 yearly XML archives, 41 monthly XML archives, 361 OCDS JSON files, 3 PDFs. XML and OCDS overlap from June 2021 to May 2024, so ingesting both double-counts. Depenses is the most audit-relevant file SEAO publishes: supplementary spending above 10% of the contract, with a stated reason.

sources.name: GC InfoBase
sources.covers: Federal financial, people, and results data: authorities, expenditures, spending by vote, FTEs, program-level results.
sources.format_notes: The named dataset is the index of all InfoBase CSVs. No scraping of the InfoBase UI is needed or wanted.
sources.update_cadence: with Estimates and Public Accounts cycles
sources.notes: Verified: 48 CSV resources, English/French pairs of 24 tables. Expenditures by standard object and authorities/expenditures by vote are ingested. FY2024-25 expenditures $474.4B, of which $297.1B transfer payments. InfoBase restates history for departmental mergers, so its series must not be mixed with unadjusted Public Accounts.

sources.name: Proactive disclosure — contracts over $10k
sources.covers: Federal contracts above $10,000, by department, vendor, value, and procurement method.
sources.notes: The federal counterpart to SEAO. Vendor names are free text and not keyed to a business number, so supplier-level joins need fuzzy matching.

sources.name: Proactive disclosure — grants and contributions
sources.covers: Federal grant and contribution awards by recipient, program, and value.
sources.notes: Transfer payments are about 60% of federal spending, so this is where the money actually is — but this dataset covers only the grants and contributions slice, not major statutory transfers like OAS or the Canada Health Transfer, which appear only in Estimates and Public Accounts.

sources.name: Public Accounts of Canada
sources.covers: Audited annual actuals for the Government of Canada.
sources.notes: Much of this overlaps the GC InfoBase CSVs — check InfoBase before doing PDF extraction work. Worth hunting for Excel annexes first.

sources.name: Main and Supplementary Estimates
sources.covers: What Parliament authorizes each year, by organization and vote.
sources.update_cadence: Main in spring, Supplementary A/B/C through the year
sources.notes: Authorities, not expenditures — what was approved, not what was spent. Lapsed spending is the difference and is itself worth surfacing.

sources.name: Parliamentary Budget Officer
sources.covers: Independent analysis and costing of federal fiscal policy.
sources.notes: Low volume, easy to crawl: walk the publications index for metadata and attachment links, then extract. Independent of Finance Canada, so the spread between PBO and departmental projections is informative on its own.

sources.name: Budget du Québec — Plan budgétaire
sources.covers: The annual Quebec budget: revenue, expenditure, and fiscal framework.
sources.notes: Consistent layout year to year, so table extraction is workable with per-document templates. Check for Excel annexes before writing a PDF parser.

sources.name: Budget de dépenses (Conseil du trésor)
sources.covers: Quebec expenditure budget broken down by portefeuille ministériel and by programme.
sources.notes: Previously recorded here as PDF-only requiring table extraction — that was wrong. The CSV carries PORTEFEUILLE / PROGRAMME / ELEMENT / SUPERCATEGORIE / TYPE_DE_CREDITS, which is the full expenditure taxonomy. 2026-27: $145.5B of crédits across 25 portefeuilles, 99 programmes and 330 éléments.
sources.format_notes: CSV on Données Québec, four tables per year back to 2019-20: budgets et crédits des ministères, crédits de transfert, crédits aux fonds spéciaux, and prévisions des organismes autres que budgétaires. The PDF volumes carry the same figures with commentary.

sources.name: Comptes publics du Québec
sources.notes: Published as CSV on Données Québec in two volumes, not PDF-only as previously recorded here. Volume 2 carries expenditure detail — the actuals to set against the Budget de dépenses plan.

sources.name: Données Québec
sources.covers: Quebec open data portal, including many municipalities. Host for the SEAO release files.
sources.license: varies by publisher, mostly Open Government Licence – Québec
sources.notes: Same CKAN API shape as open.canada.ca, so one client covers both portals.

sources.name: Vérificateur général du Québec
sources.covers: Audits of Quebec government spending, including findings of mismanagement.
sources.notes: The qualitative counterpart to the expenditure data — where the money went wrong. Low volume: crawl the publications index, then extract.

caveats.summary: Federal and Quebec consolidate at different levels, so economic categories that look equivalent are not. Federal Personnel is $65.3B; Quebec Rémunération is $4.9B — because Quebec's public-sector payroll sits inside the $112.1B it books as Transfert to the health and education networks, which employ the staff. Charting 'personnel spending' side by side compares a consolidated figure with an unconsolidated one. govbudget.taxonomy flags this per category: only debt service is freely comparable.

The Budget de dépenses and Comptes publics are published as CSV on Données Québec, not only as PDF. This registry previously recorded them as requiring table extraction, which overstated the remaining work substantially — the Quebec expenditure taxonomy is directly machine-readable.

SEAO's two eras overlap in content, not only in file dates. Splitting the backfill at 2021-05 stops the files overlapping, but OCDS releases still republish awards the XML era already carried, under a different award_id — and the NEQ is present in one era and absent in the other, so any key built from those fields changes shape at the boundary and never matches itself. Measured on the full 17-year dataset this double-counted 20.4% of the total: $117.6B of $576.6B. Identity must be resolved economically (notice, supplier, amount, award date), which brings the total to $463.0B.

8,432 awards carry an amount of $1 or less and a further 16,000 are under $1,000. These are placeholders for open-ended or unit-price contracts, not real values. Any ratio computed against them — an overrun percentage, a variance — produces figures in the billions of percent. Guard the denominator.

Some individual awards carry amounts that are clearly source data-entry errors: one municipal waste régie appears at $8.83B, roughly 1.9% of the entire 17-year total, alongside a $4.55M award on the same notice. The top 10 awards are 4.3% of the total, so a single bad row visibly moves headline figures. Outliers should be surfaced, not silently trimmed.

Parallel float summation is not associative, so an unrounded SUM over ~900k rows varies in its last decimals between runs of identical data, and rounding only moves the coin-flip to the half-cent boundary. Money is summed as DECIMAL, and every window function and LIMIT carries a total ordering, so the published aggregates are byte-reproducible.

SEAO's <fournisseurs> block lists every bidder, not just the winner. Only <adjudicataire>1</adjudicataire> is an award. On May 2024 data that is 6,276 winners out of 11,350 bidder rows — treating all rows as awards overstates contract spending by roughly 80%. The OCDS era publishes winners only, so both parsers set is_winner and every total must filter on it.

<montantssoumisunite> says what an amount is denominated in: dollars, but also $/km, $/hour, %, points and $US. Summing without filtering adds percentages to dollars. Only units 0 and 1 are plain CAD. Code 0 is absent from the published specification but is the most common value and matches the independently published final amounts at a median ratio of 1.000, so it is treated as dollars.

SEAO writes 0.000000 rather than an empty element for 'not applicable'. <montanttotalcontrat> is usually 0 while <montantcontrat> holds the real figure, so straightforward field-preference ordering silently picks zero.

Awarded, final and supplementary amounts are three different numbers published in three different files (Avis, Contrats, Depenses), joined on numeroseao. The awarded amount is not what was ultimately paid. Cost overruns are only visible by joining Depenses back to the award.

The two eras label procurement methods differently — the XML <type> code table gives 'Contrat octroyé de gré à gré' while OCDS procurementMethodDetails gives 'Contrat de gré à gré'. Grouping by method across eras splits one category in two until a crosswalk is applied.

Some Government of Canada hosts (tpsgc-pwgsc.gc.ca among them) serve certificates under Entrust roots, which Mozilla distrusted in 2024 and certifi therefore no longer ships. Python clients using certifi cannot reach them even though browsers can. The project defers to the OS trust store via the truststore package rather than weakening verification.

The federal standard object / vote / program taxonomy and Quebec's portefeuille / mission / programme taxonomy do not map onto each other. There is no crosswalk that survives contact with the detail. Either build two parallel fact tables joined only at a coarse function level, or accept lossy mapping into one — but decide before writing the schema, because retrofitting is expensive.

Organizations are merged, split, and renamed across years in both jurisdictions. GC InfoBase already restates its historical series to account for this; raw Public Accounts does not. Mixing an adjusted series with an unadjusted one produces phantom jumps at reorganization boundaries.

Estimates report authorities (what Parliament approved), Public Accounts report expenditures (what was spent). The gap is lapsed spending and is real, not error. Never sum or chart the two without labels.

SEAO changed from yearly XML to OCDS-based JSON in March 2021. Field semantics differ, not just the encoding. Ingest the overlap window from both sides once and diff it before trusting a unified contract series across that boundary.

Transfer payments are roughly 60% of federal expenditure, but the proactive-disclosure grants dataset covers only grants and contributions. Major statutory transfers — OAS/GIS, the Canada Health Transfer — appear only in Estimates and Public Accounts. A dashboard built solely on disclosure data will understate federal spending by a wide margin.

Federal transfers to Quebec appear as federal expenditure and again as Quebec revenue funding Quebec expenditure. Summing federal and provincial spending double-counts the Canada Health Transfer and equalization. Consolidated totals must net out intergovernmental transfers or clearly present the two levels separately.

Federal contract disclosure records vendor names as free text with no business number. SEAO carries the NEQ for Quebec suppliers. Cross-jurisdiction supplier analysis therefore needs fuzzy matching and should carry a confidence score rather than implying certainty.

Both the federal government and Quebec run April 1 to March 31, which is a rare convenience — but municipal entities in the SEAO data often use the calendar year. Do not assume a single fiscal calendar across the contract data.

Most of this is under the Open Government Licence (Canada or Québec), which permits commercial reuse but requires attribution. Anything public-facing needs a visible attribution statement per the licence terms.

Quebec sources are French-first and some federal datasets carry parallel English and French columns. Normalize on one language for keys while retaining both for display, or joins will silently fail on accented and translated variants.
